jtbd_records.job_statement: View pipeline logs for troubleshooting and audits
jtbd_records.context: When I need to review and analyze pipeline activity
jtbd_records.outcome: So I can troubleshoot issues and conduct audits without depending on pod retention
jtbd_records.current_heading: Viewing pipeline logs by using the OpenShift Logging Operator

evidence.direct_quote: Pipeline runs, task runs, and event listeners store their logs in their pods. It is useful to review and analyze logs for troubleshooting and audits.

jtbd_records.job_statement: Avoid resource waste from indefinite pod retention
jtbd_records.context: When I need to retain logs but don't want to keep pods running
jtbd_records.outcome: So I can reduce unnecessary resource consumption and avoid cluttered namespaces
jtbd_records.current_heading: Viewing pipeline logs by using the OpenShift Logging Operator

evidence.direct_quote: However, retaining the pods indefinitely leads to unnecessary resource consumption and cluttered namespaces.

jtbd_records.job_statement: View pipeline logs using Elasticsearch Kibana stack
jtbd_records.context: When I need to access pipeline logs after pods are deleted
jtbd_records.outcome: So I can review logs without dependency on pod availability
jtbd_records.current_heading: Viewing pipeline logs by using the OpenShift Logging Operator

evidence.direct_quote: To remove any dependency on the pods for viewing pipeline logs, you can use the OpenShift Elasticsearch Operator and the OpenShift Logging Operator. These Operators help you to view pipeline logs by using the Elasticsearch Kibana stack, even after you have deleted the pods that contained the logs.

jtbd_records.job_statement: Access pipeline logs in Kibana web console
jtbd_records.context: When I prefer a graphical interface over command-line
jtbd_records.outcome: So I can view and analyze pipeline logs through a visual interface

evidence.direct_quote: You can view pipeline logs by using the Kibana web console instead of the command-line interface. Use the following procedure to access the logs.

jtbd_records.job_statement: Create an index pattern in Kibana
jtbd_records.context: When I need to set up Kibana to display pipeline logs
jtbd_records.outcome: So I can configure the time-based index for log viewing

evidence.direct_quote: Create an index pattern: On the left navigation panel of the Kibana web console, click Management. Click Create index pattern. Under Step 1 of 2: Define index pattern → Index pattern, enter a * pattern and click Next Step. Under Step 2 of 2: Configure settings → Time filter field name, select @timestamp from the drop-down menu, and click Create index pattern.

jtbd_records.context: When I need to narrow down logs to specific pipelines or components
jtbd_records.outcome: So I can focus on relevant pipeline execution logs
jtbd_records.line_reference: → Lines 107-170: Add filter steps with examples

evidence.direct_quote: Add a filter: On the left navigation panel of the Kibana web console, click Discover. Click Add a filter + → Edit Query DSL.

jtbd_records.job_statement: Display and read pipeline log messages
jtbd_records.context: When I need to view the actual log content
jtbd_records.outcome: So I can read and analyze specific log messages from pipeline runs
jtbd_records.line_reference: → Lines 173-179: Select fields and view messages

evidence.direct_quote: From the Available fields list, select the following fields: kubernetes.flat_labels, message. Ensure that the selected fields appear under the Selected fields list. The message field displays the logs.
